question: Why are the QC procedures for PRS more conservative than for a single-SNP analysis?

answers.answer: Small errors can be amplified across the many variants summed into the score
answers.feedback: Right. A PRS adds up thousands to millions of SNPs, so systematic errors accumulate.

answers.answer: PRS software cannot handle missing genotypes
answers.feedback: Missing genotypes can be handled. The reason for caution is that errors add up across the score.

answers.answer: PRS are only calculated for rare variants

question: A GWAS of a trait reports h²SNP = 0.02. According to the tutorial's recommendation, should you build a PRS from it?

answers.answer: No — the recommendation is to use GWAS with h²SNP > 0.05
answers.feedback: Right. With so little variance explained by common SNPs, the PRS would have very low predictive power.
A PRS cannot explain more than the SNP-heritability, so 0.02 sets a very low ceiling. The tutorial recommends h²SNP > 0.05.

answers.answer: Yes, as long as the target sample has more than 100 people
answers.feedback: A larger target sample helps power, but it cannot raise the ceiling set by low heritability.

question: Which of these SNPs is strand-ambiguous?

answers.feedback: Right. C pairs with G, so a C/G SNP reads C/G on both strands, and the effect allele cannot be confirmed from the alleles alone. A/T SNPs have the same problem.
On the other strand C/T reads G/A, which is distinguishable. Only A/T and C/G SNPs are ambiguous.
A/G on one strand is T/C on the other, which is distinguishable.

question: Base data are on GRCh37 and target data on GRCh38. What should you do?

answers.answer: Convert one data set to the other build (for example with liftOver) before matching variants
answers.feedback: Right. The same SNP has different positions on different builds, so positions must be converted first.

answers.answer: Nothing — rsIDs and positions are the same on every build
answers.feedback: Positions change between builds, and matching by position would fail or mismatch.

question: Why must there be no sample overlap between base and target data?

answers.answer: Overlapping people make the PRS look more predictive than it really is
answers.feedback: Right. Their own data helped estimate the weights, so the score over-fits them.

answers.answer: Overlapping people make the PRS look less predictive
answers.feedback: Overlap inflates, not deflates, apparent performance.

answers.answer: It is a privacy rule with no statistical effect
answers.feedback: Overlap has a real statistical effect: over-fitting.
